opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's going to be both, and they're complementary rather than competing. The large frontier models will keep pushing what's possible: reasoning, complex multi-step tasks, the really hard problems. That's important, and it's where a lot of new capabilities first show up.

But once a capability exists, there's a strong pull toward compressing it. We saw it again and again over the last couple of years. Something that needed a huge model one year can be done surprisingly well by a model ten or a hundred times smaller a year or two later, through distillation, better data, and better training recipes. Data quality in particular turned out to matter far more than people expected.

So I picture a kind of layered ecosystem. The big models act almost like teachers, or like the place you go for the hardest queries. Then a whole long tail of smaller models runs locally, on your laptop, your phone, eventually your robot. Those are cheaper, faster, private, and you can actually own them, fine-tune them, and understand what they're doing. For a lot of companies that control matters a lot. You don't always want to send your data to an API, and you don't want your product to break because someone else changed a model behind the scenes.

I'm also excited about systems where the two work together: a small local model handles most things and knows when to call a bigger one. That's how a lot of agentic setups will end up looking, I think.

And from an open-source perspective, small models are where the community can really participate. Not everyone can train a frontier model, but lots of people can train, tweak, and share a one- or three-billion-parameter model. That's where you get a huge diversity of experimentation, and historically that's where a lot of the good ideas come from.

r001.rationale: The candidate says large frontier models and smaller local models are complementary and describes both having roles in a layered ecosystem.

r002.rationale: It says a small local model can handle most things while a larger model handles the hardest queries, communicating that the largest model is not best for every task.

r003.rationale: The candidate mentions reasoning, complex multi-step tasks, and hard problems, but does not identify prolonged reflection as a reason to use much larger models.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So I think the honest answer is that it's not really a competition, it's a division of labor that's going to settle out over the next few years, and we're already seeing the shape of it.

The very large frontier models are going to keep being the place where new capabilities first appear. Every time someone trains a bigger model with more compute, we discover something it can do that nobody explicitly designed for. That's not going away. But those models are expensive to run, they live in a datacenter, you send your data to someone else, and for most actual tasks people do day to day, they're massively overpowered. You don't need a thousand-billion-parameter model to summarize your email or fill in a form or do speech recognition on your phone.

What's been striking to me at Hugging Face is how fast capabilities migrate downward. Something that required the biggest model in the world eighteen months ago, you can now distill into a model that fits on a laptop, sometimes on a phone. And that happens through a few mechanisms: better data, better training recipes, distillation from the big models themselves, and just the community iterating very quickly in the open. So the frontier keeps moving, but the gap between the frontier and what's cheap and local keeps compressing.

So my picture of the mature ecosystem is something like what happened with computing generally. You have the cloud, you have the edge, and you route tasks to where they make sense. A small model on your device handles the private stuff, the low-latency stuff, the things where you just don't want a round trip to a server. And when you hit something genuinely hard, you escalate to a big model. We're already seeing systems built this way, with routers or agents deciding which model to call.

And I'd add one thing, which is that the small, open models matter enormously for who gets to participate. If the only useful AI is a handful of giant proprietary models, then research, product building, and understanding of these systems is concentrated in a few labs. Small open models are what let a university lab, a startup in Nairobi, a hospital that can't send patient data anywhere, actually work with this technology. So I care about the small models not just because they're efficient, but because they're the democratic part of the story.

r001.rationale: Predicts a division of labor: small local models handle many tasks, with difficult tasks escalated to large models.

r002.rationale: Says frontier models are overpowered for most day-to-day tasks and gives examples that do not need them.

r003.rationale: Does not identify prolonged reflection as a reason to use much larger models.

astra-6.text:
I think we’ll have both. There’s a tendency to imagine that everything will converge on one very large model, but the constraints are different for different applications. Sometimes you want the strongest possible reasoning, and you’re happy to send a request to a large model. Sometimes you need something that runs on your phone, responds immediately, or keeps your data on your device.

The interesting question is how much capability you actually need for a particular task. A smaller model that’s adapted to your use case can be a very good choice, especially when you consider cost and latency alongside accuracy.

So I expect we’ll see systems combining these approaches: handling many requests locally and calling a larger model when necessary. And as models improve, the range of things you can do locally will grow. That makes open models particularly valuable, because people can experiment with that balance and adapt it to their own needs.

r001.rationale: The response predicts that both large models and smaller local models will remain in use, with more tasks becoming feasible locally as models improve.

r002.rationale: It says model choice depends on the task and notes that a smaller adapted model can be a good choice alongside cost and latency.

r003.rationale: The response mentions strong reasoning as a reason to use a large model, but does not identify prolonged reflection as a reason.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we’ll see both, because they serve different needs. Large foundation models are useful when you want broad capabilities and you don’t know exactly what you’re going to ask the model to do. But once you have a well-defined task, a smaller model can be much more efficient, and you can run it locally, with more control over your data and your costs.

The interesting question is how they work together. You might use a large model to help train or improve a smaller one, or have a system that handles most requests locally and calls a larger model when it needs additional capability.

So I don’t expect one model size to win. As the technology matures, I expect more diversity: different models for different constraints. And open models are important there, because they let people experiment and choose what actually works for them.

r001.rationale: The response expects both large foundation models and smaller local models to remain in use as AI matures, serving different needs.

r002.rationale: It says smaller models can be more efficient for well-defined tasks and predicts that no single model size will win.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify tasks requiring prolonged reflection as a reason to use much larger models.
